Agile delivery methodology

2 weeks

A typical sprint

Transparent communication, fast visible results to test hypotheses, and forecasts supported by planning and reporting. The process adapts as requirements change.

Product backlog

A prioritized list of product capabilities.

→

Sprint planning

Agree what to deliver and how to achieve it.

→

Sprint backlog & delivery

Build the agreed work with daily scrum coordination.

→

Definition of done

Check the criteria required to complete the work.

→

Sprint review

Review completed work and identify changes.

Feedback + retrospective shape the next sprint

Sprint retrospective

Discuss what went well and what to improve for the next sprint.

Product owner · team · scrum master

Align priorities, deliver the product and support an effective sprint process.

Content and source notes

This enterprise option is adapted from the general company introduction. All company information comes from the supplied 18-page Itexus presentation.pdf, and every substantive content block is retained except the fintech domain list, which slide 6 replaces with twelve enterprise domains drawn from the industries in the Itexus portfolio. Company figures, recognition, provider names, tools and contact links reflect that source; they have not been updated to a new reporting date.

The source describes over 130 engineers and IT specialists, 50+ senior developers, 300+ completed projects and 80+ fintech projects over ten years; 170+ refers to clients across 23 countries. It reports 94% retention, 75% of clients through referrals and 140+ partners. Client geography is 43% USA, 38% Europe and 19% other. The original recognition ribbon and Clutch 39-review artwork are preserved.

Provider and collaboration tool names are transcribed from the source artwork, including historical names such as TD Ameritrade, SynapseFI, Sendinblue, Skype and Google Hangouts. These describe the supplied experience snapshot and are not recommendations to adopt a provider today.

The discovery example’s customer-specific “Coinme application” reference is generalized to “existing application.” The source’s apparent tool typo “ESlist” is normalized to “ESLint” and “Flake 8” to “Flake8.” The unexplained partner acronym “BAA” is retained as written in the source. Project-specific scope, pricing and delivery promises from the proposal template are replaced with this company introduction.

The page-by-page content map is in SOURCE-CONTENT.md. Contact and social links are copied from the PDF’s link annotations. Photos and recognition artwork come from the supplied PDF; the theme and logo are inherited from the existing HTML template.

Visual assets and case studies

Integration wordmarks and the six collaboration app icons are recovered from the supplied PDF. SonarQube artwork comes from the official Sonar product press kit, ESLint uses its official logomark, and Bandit uses the project’s official artwork. Flake8 is represented by a labelled code-check symbol in the presentation’s line icon style.

The enterprise experience slide, Microsoft & Azure integration slide and three case studies are adapted from the Enterprise section of the Itexus portfolio (itexus.com/portfolio/#enterprise). Case figures are those published on each case page: 100,000+ invoices and $10M+ monthly payment volume (billing); up to 100,000 devices, a two-year engagement and a seven-person team (energy). The Microsoft partnership and the native Windows .NET emphasis in each case were supplied for this enterprise option and are not stated on the public case pages. Microsoft Azure, .NET and SQL Server artwork comes from itexus.com. See ENTERPRISE-VARIANT.md.
